title: Lee Chang-dong’s Films Head to Netflix Worldwide After ‘Possible Love’ Wins Silver Lion at Venice
description: Netflix will expand its lineup of Lee Chang-dong films worldwide, following the Silver Lion (Grand Jury Prize) win for “Possible Love” at the Venice
body:
Netflix will expand its lineup of Lee Chang-dong films worldwide, following the Silver Lion (Grand Jury Prize) win for “Possible Love” at the Venice Film Festival. 

	The expansion will let viewers everywhere explore titles including “Secret Sunshine” and “Peppermint Candy.”

	“Possible Love,” Lee’s first film in eight years, opens in South Korean theaters Sept. 23, followed by Australia and New Zealand on Oct. 22 and the U.K., Japan, the U.S. and Canada on Oct. 23. The film will premiere globally on Netflix on Nov. 6.
	

	Netflix has also been adding earlier Lee titles to its library in additional countries alongside the new release. “Green Fish” and “Secret Sunshine” began streaming in late August in Italy, the U.K., France, Australia and New Zealand. “Peppermint Candy” and “Oasis” joined the platform in Italy and Spain on Sept. 4. “Poetry” and “Burning” are also planned for release in markets including Japan, the U.S., Canada, Australia and New Zealand.


	Rollout timing differs by market, and some territories will get the films with subtitle options covering as many as six languages, Korean among them.

	Lee debuted as a director with “Green Fish” in 1997, going on to build a filmography that also includes “Peppermint Candy,” “Oasis,” “Secret Sunshine,” “Poetry” and “Burning.” His work has drawn top honors on the festival circuit: “Oasis” earned him a directing prize at Venice in 2002, and “Poetry” took the screenplay award at Cannes in 2010. Lee’s newest distinction came at the Toronto Film Festival‘s 51st edition, where he became the first Korean filmmaker to receive its Ebert Director Award.
	

	“Possible Love” centers on two couples: one formed by a man who has lost his job and his wife, the other by a woman who directs documentaries and her husband. Their lives intersect during the making of a documentary, drawing out desires and struggles each had kept hidden. The film stars Jeon Do-yeon, Sul Kyung-gu, Zo In-sung and Cho Yeo-jeong, and is South Korea’s submission for the best international feature film category at the 99th Academy Awards.

title: Hyun Bin, Lee Min-ho, Jung Woo-sung, Isabelle Huppert Headline Busan Open Talk and Outdoor Stage Greeting Lineup
description: The 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) has unveiled the lineup and schedule for three of its fan-facing programs: Open Talk, Outdoor Stag
body:
The 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) has unveiled the lineup and schedule for three of its fan-facing programs: Open Talk, Outdoor Stage Greeting and Talk-to-Talk. Held at the Busan Cinema Center Roof Theater and the HANMAC Smooooth Lounge, the sessions give audiences a chance to meet directors and cast members from a wide range of Korean and international selections. 

	Open Talk opens Oct. 7 with director Lee Chang-dong and stars Jeon Do-yeon, Sul Kyung-gu, Zo In-sung and Cho Yeo-jeong for “Possible Love,” followed by “Cattle Run,” bringing director Kim Ji-hyun together with Ryu Seung-ryong, Park Hae-jun, Ong Seong-wu and Lee Sang-hee, and “The Table: Day and Night,” pairing director Kim Jong-kwan with Kim Min-ha, Joo Jong-hyuk, Han Sun-hwa, Shim Eun-kyung, Jeon So-young and Kim Dong-hwi. 
	

	On Oct. 8, “Sapiens” brings out director Lee Hu-bin with Jung Sung-il, You Chea-myung and Ryu Hyunkyung, while “Dead-End Job” pairs director Kim Da-min with Kim Min-ha and Choi Hyun-wook. Oct. 9 sessions include “The Blue Road,” with director Han Jun-hee alongside Son Sukku, Nagayama Eita and Kim Shin-rok; “Ugly Duckling Ms. Maeng,” with director Lee Yong-jae and stars Lee Sun-bin, You Chea-myung, Jun Suk-ho and Kim Young-min; and “The Sorry Generation,” with director Kim Sung-yoon and actors Jung Jae-young, Kim Joo-ryoung, Lee Yi-kyung and Kim Ah-young. 


	A “BIFF Discoveries: Rising New Talents” session on Oct. 10 features Jeon So-young and Kim Dong-hwi from “The Table: Day and Night” alongside Sim Su-bin, who appears in both “The Birds” and “The World Before.” The program closes Oct. 13 with Isabelle Huppert and director Marc Fitoussi discussing their collaboration on “All About Corinne.”
	

	Outdoor Stage Greeting runs Oct. 7 through Oct. 11 and covers dozens of titles. On Oct. 7, director Stephanie Ahn appears with Moon Choi and Son Sukku for “Bedford Park”; director Fujii Michihito and actor Yokohama Ryusei present “You, Like a Star”; director Sato Sakichi brings Sawajiri Erika and Maruyama Ryuhei for “The Chain of Roses”; director Hur Jin-ho appears with Yoo Hai-jin, Park Hae-il and Lee Min-ho for “The Assassin(s)”; director Feng-I Fiona Roan brings Shuhua Yeh, Xuan Chen and Kent Tsai for “Happily Ever After”; director Woo Min-ho appears with Hyun Bin, Jung Woo-sung and Woo Do-hwan for “Made In Korea” Season 2; and director Kore-eda Hirokazu presents “Look Back” with Deguchi Natsuki, Makita Aju, Nanase Furi and Okada Rokka. 

	Oct. 8 brings director July Jung with Kim Doyeon and Choi Wonyoung for “Dora”; director Kim Joung-hoon with Kim Jae-won, Cho Yi-hyun, Kang You-seok and Bae Gang-hee for “Final Interview”; a second “BIFF Discoveries” session featuring Kim Doyeon from “Dora”; director Hong Sung-min with Jung Sung-il and Park Ji-hyun for “Sinner”; director Song Il-gon with Kim Hye-ja, Park Seo-kyung, Choi Ju-eun, Moon Seong-hyun and Lee Seyoung for “Still Shining”; director Kamila Andini and producer Ifa Isfansyah with Putri Marino, Christine Hakim and Arya Saloka for “Four Seasons in Java”; director Takemura Kentaro with Michieda Shunsuke and Anzai Seira for “In the Clear Moonlit Dusk”; and actors Michelle Mao and Jin Ha for “zi.” 

	Oct. 9 features director Yeon Sang-ho with Kim Hyun-joo for “Paradise Lost”; director Wang I-fan with Fukushi Sota and Han Ning for “The Scar-Faced Cat: Way of Asura”; and director Yoon Dan-bi with Sim Su-bin and Kim Eo-jin for “The World Before.” Oct. 10 brings actors Shin Mina, Ju Jihoon, Lee Jongsuk and Lee Seyoung for “The Remarried Empress,” plus Kwon Haehyo and Park Miso for “Nowhere to Lay My Eyes.” 

	The section wraps Oct. 11 with an “Italy’s Fearsome New Directors” session pairing “Föa – Once Upon a Future” director Margherita Ferrari and producer Raffaele Perillo with “Deep Blue” director Ernesto Maria Censori, actor Andrea Arcangeli, producer Giorgio Gucci, screenwriter Lorenzo Marinelli and editor Chicchi Tadeucci; “Inherit,” with director Banjong Pisanthanakun and actors Davika Hoorne and Thitiya Jirapornsilp; and a joint stage greeting for Flash Forward section directors Rhys Marc Jones, Jannis Lenz, Fernanda Tovar, Jacqueline Lentzou, Emmanuel Marre, Manuel Wetscher, Margherita Ferrari, Grzegorz Dębowski and Manuela Martelli.
	

	Talk-to-Talk splits between the Roof Theater and the HANMAC Smooooth Lounge. At the Roof Theater on Oct. 10, “Women Directors: Taking the Scene” gathers Margherita Ferrari, Marjan Khosravi, May El-Youkhy, Michelle Zhou, Zainab Entezar, Jacqueline Lentzou and Julie Lecoustre. At the HANMAC Smooooth Lounge, Majid Majidi discusses his career from “Children of Heaven” to “Midday Meal” on Oct. 9, followed by four “Vision Korea” panels on Oct. 10 and Oct. 11 connecting directors and actors from “Things I Left at the Theater,” “Not for You” and “The Flower”; “Earbug,” “Some Detective” and “Nothing Has Happened Yet”; “The Birds,” “Space” and “Cosmic Trace”; and “Baler,” “Beyond Love’s Horizon” and “Full Moon.” 

	A session titled “Asian Cinema Through Global Eyes” brings together Martine Therouanne of the Vesoul International Festival of Asian Cinema, Sabrina Baracetti of the Udine Far East Film Festival, Jeon Hyejung of the London East Asia Film Festival, Samuel Jamier of the New York Asian Film Festival and Teruoka Sozo of the Osaka Asian Film Festival. Directors Marco Nguyen and Nicolas Athané appear for “The Hottest Virus of the Year, ‘Jim Queen,'” and the program closes Oct. 13 with Kim Ah-young and Kim Seulki discussing their move from “SNL Korea” to film.

	The 31st Busan International Film Festival will run Oct. 6-15 at the Busan Cinema Center and venues throughout Busan, with the 21st Asian Contents & Film Market held Oct. 10-13.

title: Cynthia Erivo’s Riveting ‘Prima Facie’ Performance Earns TIFF Standing Ovation
description: Cynthia Erivo already earned two best actress Oscar nominations for portraying Harriet Tubman and the green-skinned Elphaba in “Wicked” — not to men
body:
Cynthia Erivo already earned two best actress Oscar nominations for portraying Harriet Tubman and the green-skinned Elphaba in “Wicked” — not to mention her Tony-winning work in “The Color Purple” — but her latest film, “Prima Facie,” might be her most challenging high-wire act yet.

	She pulled it off, according to the audience at the Toronto International Film Festival on Sunday night. “Prima Facie” held its world premiere at the Roy Thompson Hall, where the crowed rewarded Erivo and her filmmakers with a standing ovation for the harrowing drama. 
	

	Erivo plays Tessa, a rising legal star in London who represents defendants of sexual assault. When she’s raped by a colleague, the lawyer finds herself at odds with the patriarchal legal system she so often used to win. 


	White (“Bleak House,” “Jane Eyre,” “Woman Walks Ahead”) directed the adaptation by playwright Suzie Miller from her globally acclaimed one-woman show. The film is one of the hottest sales titles on the block at TIFF. 

	Jodie Comer won the Tony and Olivier awards for the stage version, and Erivo proved equally captivating on the big screen — albeit under a a very racial and socioeconomic context.  Erivo’s Tessa is a woman of color from a working class background, navigating a system bolstered by white men dating back to medieval times in the London court. 

	“We got the chance to meet a lot of Black women barristers. I understood that they sort of work in a different rhythm to everybody else, and the way they approach court is very much making it their own,” Erivo said at a Q&A following the premiere  “I wanted that for Tessa, I wanted her to have this outside life that influenced the way she approached [her work].” 
	

	Also featured among the supporting cast are Daniel Ings, Elizabeth Dulau and Simon Russell Beale.

schema.headline: Cynthia Erivo’s Riveting ‘Prima Facie’ Performance Earns TIFF Standing Ovation

title: ‘Lanterns’ Star Poorna Jagannathan Breaks Down Zoe’s Brutal Episode 5: ‘It’s a Faustian Play She Makes’
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for “Lanterns” Episode 5, titled “Lights Out,” now streaming on HBO Max. 

	This week’s episode of “La
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for “Lanterns” Episode 5, titled “Lights Out,” now streaming on HBO Max. 

	This week’s episode of “Lanterns” finally unmasks the Manhunter, who’s been at the heart of the mystery in Rushville throughout the season.

	As revealed at the end of Episode 4, the Manhunter is in fact Zoe Macon, played by Poorna Jagannathan. In an interview with Variety, Jagannathan said that she had no idea she was the Manhunter until she got the script for the fourth episode. “Everyone saw it coming except me!” she says with a laugh.
	

	“Obviously, I’m grateful that they didn’t tell me initially, because in my audition I know I would have acted like a robot,” she says.


	The episode begins by delving into how the Manhunter holds so much sway over the people of Rushville. We see Sheriff Kerry (Kelly Macdonald) years before on the run from some gangsters to whom her father owed money. They track her to the Rushville diner, where Zoe is sitting in a booth by herself. Out of nowhere, she snaps one gangster’s neck and informs the other that he will be going back to his boss and telling him that Kerry is dead.

	Kerry is grateful, but obviously scared. Zoe explains that Kerry can have a safe and peaceful life in Rushville, so long as Kerry is willing to protect Zoe when the time comes. 

	“[Co-creator] Chris [Mundy] and Geeta Patel, the director of that episode, wanted a sense that that scene is emblematic of the contract Zoe has made with every single person in the town,” Jagannathan says. “Her survival depends on you agreeing to your survival. It’s a Faustian play she makes.”
	

	Given that, Rushville goes into high alert, as Zoe knows that Antaan (Paul Ben-Victor) and his team will be on their way to kill her. All the citizens arm themselves and prepare for battle. 

	Hal (Kyle Chandler), meanwhile, has left John (Aaron Pierre) trapped in their car after forcing him into a crash at the end of the last episode. He plans to let Antaan and Will Macon’s (Garret Dillahunt) militia shoot it out while he goes after Zoe to turn her over to the Guardians. 

	Zoe tracks John down just as the car begins to burn. But rather than save him, she waits for it to explode.  Now severely burned and barely alive, John is taken to the local hospital, where he reveals to Zoe that he knows the Guardians are the ones who created the Manhunters in the first place. 

	Zoe offers John a deal: She will heal his injuries so long as he lets Hal die and tells the Guardians that all is well. “She waits for John to burn, and he is hanging by a thread to life,” Jagannathan says. “What you understand is she waits for people to be at their most vulnerable point, near death — and she comes in to save them.”

	On why she believes Zoe wouldn’t have let John die, Jagannathan believes the character understood that having the gratitude and protection of a Green Lantern would be “her crown jewel.” 

	“She quickly assessed who is her biggest threat,” she says. “She quickly assessed who could be her strongest protector, and it wasn’t Hal — it was John. She sees something in John where she knows that he is going to be the better Green Lantern.”

	Antaan and his team reach Rushville, and Hal finds them at the diner. He tells Antaan that Will is the Manhunter, but Antaan is clearly suspicious. Still, they set off for Will’s ranch armed to the teeth. 

	Back at the hospital, John has agreed to Zoe’s terms, and she prepares to heal him using alien technology. He asks her why she chose the form of a South Asian woman, to which she replies that being an outsider allows her a “higher vantage point” from which she can infiltrate a society.

	“My outsiderness over the years has definitely become my strength,” Jagannathan says. “It’s the thing that I bring to the party. So when I read that monologue, I was like, ‘OK, that’s my in.'”

	“You just don’t get asked a lot of questions if you are presented as outsider,” she continues. “No one really knows what questions to ask you. You can hide in plain sight, and that’s the tactic she chose in order to come and live on this planet.”
	

	Now fully healed, John deduces that Zoe killed Abin Sur, the Green Lantern who passed his ring to Hal, as he was going to let her go on Earth. But Zoe couldn’t risk Abin Sur one day revealing her location to the Guardians. 

	While Jagannathan believes that all the characters in “Lanterns” are presented with a wide range of shades of gray, Zoe is ultimately a “victim of her programming” as a Manhunter.

	Antaan and his team assault Will’s ranch. He patiently waits inside for Antaan to get there, calling Zoe to thank her for giving him more time to live. Antaan arrives, and Zoe has coached Will to pretend to be the Manhunter to throw Antaan off the trail. But Antaan dispatches Will, and cuts out his heart, proving he is human.

	Zoe needs to draw Hal out, so she begins firing space-based weapons onto the town in order to force him to drain his ring’s power. He manages to find her, but she escapes. With his ring nearly drained, Hal has to return to the motel to recharge it.

	Once he arrives, John is waiting for him. He brutally assaults Hal as they begin a knockdown, drag out brawl that has been brewing since the season started. John gets the upper hand and nearly takes the ring, before one of Zoe’s satellite weapons blows up half the motel, forcing Hal to use what little charge is left in the ring to protect himself and John. 

	As the dust settles, John flees, but Zoe comes with a gun to finish off Hal in the rubble. Hal laughs, knowing that if John wanted him dead, he would have done it himself. Suddenly, we see John staring down the barrel of a sniper rifle, which is trained on Zoe. She turns around and looks at John with a softness in her eyes just before he fires.

	“John is the only person she has ever encountered that she didn’t predict,” Jagannathan says. “Everyone else has always fallen into line. I think the last look is kind of game-recognized-game. It was a complete appreciation for someone whose sense of morality outdid anything and everything, and ultimately that’s the only thing that could have killed her. Someone who broke the contract, and no one ever has.”

	John returns to the motel, takes the ring and lantern from Hal and walks through the rubble of Rushville. He goes to the local bar, where Lianna (Laura Linney) is waiting for him. Though he finally has what he’s always wanted, John walks away from Lianna, leaving the ring behind.

schema.headline: ‘Lanterns’ Star Poorna Jagannathan Breaks Down Zoe’s Brutal Episode 5: ‘It’s a Faustian Play She Makes’

title: Korea Box Office: ‘The Odyssey’ Secures Sixth Weekend Crown as ‘Obsession’ Ascends
description:
“The Odyssey” continued its voyage at the summit of the South Korean box office during the weekend of Sept. 11–13. 

	According to data from KOBIS,
body:
“The Odyssey” continued its voyage at the summit of the South Korean box office during the weekend of Sept. 11–13. 

	According to data from KOBIS, the tracking service operated by the Korean Film Council, the Christopher Nolan-directed tentpole generated $3.9 million from 449,474 admissions over the three-day frame across 1,648 screens, capturing 51.4% of the total weekend market.

	Securing its sixth consecutive weekend victory, the blockbuster pushed its cumulative South Korean gross to $89.6 million from 10,782,715 total admissions since its Aug. 5 launch.
	

	“Obsession” climbed to second place in its second weekend, pulling in $1.4 million from 176,479 admissions across 845 screens. The film accounted for 18.6% of the weekend market, lifting its cume to $3.7 million from 474,818 total viewers.


	Superhero tentpole “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” was tin third place in its seventh outing, generating $544,123 from 84,719 admissions over the frame. The film accounted for 7% of the frame, bringing its local gross to $68.7 million from 8,930,413 admissions.

	“The Drama” opened in fourth place, earning $223,340 from 29,512 admissions over the three-day window across 616 screens. Since its Sept. 9 premiere, the release has collected $404,575 from 53,631 total admissions.

	Local family road-trip drama “The Journey to Gyeongju” took fifth place, generating $124,071 from 17,206 admissions. Directed by Kim Mi-jo and starring Lee Jung-eun, Gong Hyo-jin, Park So-dam, Lee Yeon, and Byun Yo-han, the revenge-tinged family narrative pushed its haul to $2.3 million from 332,960 viewers.
	

	“Power Ballad” placed sixth, taking $110,283 from 15,277 admissions and has gathered $633,484 from 89,399 admissions since its Sept. 2 debut.

	Sci-fi thriller “Hope” rebounded into the top 10 in seventh place, adding $125,591 from 14,719 admissions. Directed by Na Hong-Jin and starring Hwang Jung-min, Zo In-sung, Jung Ho-yeon, Michael Fassbender, and Alicia Vikander, the alien-encounter feature has accumulated $36.2 million from 4,566,216 ticket buyers.

	Toho’s anime classic “Inuyasha the Movie: Affections Touching Across Time,” directed by Toshiya Shinohara, entered the chart in eighth place, earning $89,975 from 10,935 admissions across 129 screens for a cumulative $159,850 from 19,829 admissions.

	The local family crime-drama “Portrait of a Family,” directed by Lee Ji-won and starring Ryu Seung-ryong and Ha Ji-won, finished in ninth place with $66,614 from 9,752 admissions over the weekend, moving its cume to $652,858 from 97,145 viewers. Directed by Lee Ji-won and starring Ryu Seung-ryong and Ha Ji-won, the film centers on a former superstar baseball player and a top actress whose glamorous lives unravel when a mysterious young girl appears, dragging them into a desperate struggle seven years later. 

	Rounding out the top 10 was the upcoming animated adventure “Forgotten Island,” which took $70,125 from 9,314 admissions across early festival and special preview screenings, lifting its pre-release total to $88,051 from 11,772 viewers ahead of its wide launch on Sep. 23.

	The overall market collective gross for the weekend was $7.6 million, down from last week’s $9.8 million.

schema.headline: Korea Box Office: ‘The Odyssey’ Secures Sixth Weekend Crown as ‘Obsession’ Ascends

title: ‘All That She Wants’ Review: Annie Murphy and Cooper Raiff Are Well-Matched in a Generation-Gap Romcom
description: Millennials get their Mrs. Robinson moment with “All That She Wants,” an age-gap romcom titled after the 1992 Ace of Base hit. If you remember liste
body:
Millennials get their Mrs. Robinson moment with “All That She Wants,” an age-gap romcom titled after the 1992 Ace of Base hit. If you remember listening to that song on a cassingle, it’s time to ask your doctor about perimenopause. Professional dancer Emma (Annie Murphy) isn’t quite there yet, but in her early thirties, she’s feeling her age. Symptoms include baby fever, exacerbated by the pregnancy announcement of her sister Macy (Zosia Mamet), and an intolerance to her pompous, long-term but non-committal boyfriend Spencer (Finn Wittrock).
	

	In the wake of her breakup, Emma meets an intriguing guy, Luke (Cooper Raiff), at a nightclub. A grad student, he’s about a decade younger than Emma, but his old soul is enchanted by her awkward manic pixie dream girl energy. Fueled by shots and undeniable chemistry, they fall into bed in his university dorm room. Here’s the twist: In the clarity of morning, Emma spots a few family photos and realizes she used to babysit four year-old Luke, whom she once referred to as “Lil Lukey.”


	“Schitt’s Creek” writer David West Read penned this script specifically for Murphy, who won an Emmy for her performance in that acclaimed comedy series, and the film is built around the expressive physical humor that made her Alexis Rose so GIF-able. But “All That She Wants” gives Murphy an opportunity to demonstrate her dramatic chops too, in a role that requires Emma to grow over time, which is marked over a couple of years in jumps from May to December (LOL).

	The film is co-directed by spouses Andrew Rhymer and (in her helming debut) Scarlett Bermingham, who previously worked on the 2019 wedding rom-com “Plus One” — Rhymer as co-writer and co-director, Bermingham as a supporting player. While the tone and look of “All That She Wants” starts out quite Netflix-y, it’s the characters and performances that elevate this to future comfort-watch territory.
	

	In his own films as director-star, Raiff has made himself the go-to younger guy for age-gap romances. His college-set debut “Shithouse” was about the connection between a freshman and his sophomore resident advisor (Dylan Gelula); he followed that up with “Cha Cha Real Smooth,” playing a bar mitzvah party-starter flirting with an older single mom played by Dakota Johnson. However, Raiff is a far more appealing romantic lead under the guidance of a different directing team, with another writer’s script. This is his warmest and most charming turn yet — his edges buffed out in a good way.

	While the former babysitter hiccup is ostensibly the obstacle for Emma and Charlie’s love story, Emma gets over it pretty quickly, and that speed bump is a little too contrived and minor. The biggest hurdle is Emma’s own brain. She’s hamstrung herself with the toxic perfectionism she inherited from her mother (Christine Baranski), and the expectations that she perceives other people have for her. The title “All that She Wants” might be a little cutesy (that needle-drop is both inevitable and highly anticipated), but it’s also apt. What exactly does Emma want for herself that has nothing to do with what other people have decided she should want?

	Like the maneater protagonist of the song, what Emma wants is a baby — an actual human child —whether that’s considered feminist or not. She throws herself into a career change, but her desire for motherhood doesn’t abate, and she realizes that Luke might be an ideal sperm donor. He agrees because he wants to help, and to spend time with Emma. Within the confines of this transactional relationship, will Emma let herself love Luke? Or be loved by him?

	Murphy and Raiff are well-matched. Emma’s manic, quirky energy might feel slightly out of date and a little over the top, but that’s what makes Luke adore her, and because we see her through his eyes, she’s perfectly adorkable. Luke grounds Emma, but ultimately, Emma grounds herself, through purpose and family. It’s satisfying seeing the journey that this character goes on to finding her own happiness, as much within herself as with others.

	Rhymer and Bermingham’s solid direction lets the performances shine against a standard-issue, spit-shiny Toronto landscape. But “All That She Wants” is more about the script. Read kicks this tale off with a meet-cute and an unconventional relationship, but finds authentic emotion and real social issues to power the characters’ journeys forward. As the anecdotal data piles up — from cultural trend pieces, to pop culture, to movies like “Babygirl” and “I Want Your Sex” — it’s no surprise that the younger man-older woman dynamic has made its way to the romantic comedy. This time, “Mrs. Robinson” finds a different, more modern kind of happy ending.

schema.headline: ‘All That She Wants’ Review: Annie Murphy and Cooper Raiff Are Well-Matched in a Generation-Gap Romcom

title: China Box Office: ‘Once Upon a Time in the Middle East’ Stays on Top as ‘The Odyssey’ Crosses $100 Million
description: Dirty Monkeys’ war comedy-drama “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” held the number one spot at the mainland China box office for the fifth straig
body:
Dirty Monkeys’ war comedy-drama “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” held the number one spot at the mainland China box office for the fifth straight frame, collecting RMB52.9 million ($7.8 million) over the Sept. 11–13 weekend, according to data from Artisan Gateway. 

	Directed by Wen Muye (“Dying to Survive”) and starring Shen Teng, Jiang Qiming, Aarif Rahman, and Omar Sherif, the late-summer hit has lifted its cume to $318.4 million since opening on Aug. 11. The story tracks a Chinese chef who travels to the Middle East to run an eatery to clear family debts, only for his establishment to turn into a vital haven for civilians and orphans after regional armed conflict erupts.
	

	Pearl River Film Group’s crime thriller “V” took second place in its fourth weekend of release, taking in $4.7 million. Directed by Han Yan (“Love Never Ends”) and featuring an ensemble led by Tony Leung Ka-fai, Zhu Yilong, Tan Jianci, and Kara Wai, the gritty production has now amassed $84.1 million since rolling out on Aug. 19.


	Pearl Studio’s animated fantasy comedy “All Wishes Come True!” was in third position in its ninth frame, generating $4 million. Directed by Mu Zhengyang, the enduring family hit has reached a cumulative total of $283.4 million since its July 18 debut.

	In fourth place Universal’s “The Odyssey” crossed the century mark in China, adding $3.5 million for a cumulative total of $102.9 million. Crossing the $100 million threshold pushes the film well past the China runs of “Oppenheimer,” “Tenet,” and “Inception,” leaving it second in Christopher Nolan’s local catalog only to the $122 million lifetime gross of “Interstellar.”
	

	Rounding out the top five, Phoenix Legend Films’ time-bending fantasy romance “My Tomorrow, Your Yesterday” opened with $1.7 million over its two-day debut frame. Directed by Xiang Guoqiang and adapted from Takafumi Nanatsuki’s Japanese novel, the film stars Bi Wenjun as an architectural restorer who falls in love with a medical student played by He Landou, only to uncover that her timeline flows in reverse to his, leaving them with an expiring window together.

	Mainland China’s overall weekend grosses reached $28.8 million, while the 2026 year-to-date box office stands at $4.26 billion, down 27.6% from the same period in 2025.

schema.headline: China Box Office: ‘Once Upon a Time in the Middle East’ Stays on Top as ‘The Odyssey’ Crosses $100 Million

title: ‘Pretenders’ Review: A Superb Portrait of Chrissie Hynde and Her Legendary Band Captures Their Incandescence…and Tragedy
description: As a rock star, Chrissie Hynde has always been a bit of a paradox — gnarly but cerebral, ferocious yet guarded. And “Pretenders,” Joss Crowley’s sen
body:
As a rock star, Chrissie Hynde has always been a bit of a paradox — gnarly but cerebral, ferocious yet guarded. And “Pretenders,” Joss Crowley’s sensational and revealing music documentary, shows you that there was a paradox — a glorious one — built into her band.

	Formed in London in 1978, the Pretenders emerged from the moment when “punk” had morphed into “new wave.” But there were still musicians around who could claim to be both, and Hynde was one of them. When you listen to “Precious,” which is totally a punk song (it has the potent high-speed sizzle of something by the Ramones), the ice-cold defiance and gutter snarl of Hynde’s singing (“Made me wanna…”), the song’s total fuck-it-all vibe, are undiminished by time. Hynde, with her shag haircut and androgynous toothy scowl, had emerged from the original punk scene (she’d moved to London in her early 20s and even tried to join the Slits), and it left its mark on her. She was a blistering rocker who was going to be no one’s doll.  
	

	And yet…as fierce and defining as a song like “Precious” was, it doesn’t represent what I ultimately cherish about the Pretenders. To say what that is, I have to use a word that risks sounding innocuous: They were tuneful. They came out of the world of rage and nihilism and buzzcuts and heroin, but there was an incandescence to the songs Hynde wrote, and to how the band sounded. For years, rock critics of the post-new wave era struggled to come up with different words to communicate the concept of “jangly guitar.” But it was James Honeyman-Scott, the lead guitarist of the Pretenders, who owned jangly guitar, and in some ways invented it. He had a sound that rang. And Hynde, though she had the feeling of punk in her bones, was the most romantic songwriter of that scene. I don’t mean romantic as in “love songs,” but as in conjuring the majestic romanticism of life. Just listen to “Kid,” a song so happy and sad at the same time that it’s worthy of the Beatles.
	

	“Pretenders,” which is built around astonishing archival footage as well as a lengthy interview with Hynde (Crowley also talks to many fascinating people in her orbit), is a movie that understands that side of the Pretenders — that they were making music so shimmering in its timelessness that it transcended the new-wave aesthetic and a lot of other things. How Chrissie Hynde wound up being that kind of songwriter is anyone’s guess. Songwriting is one of the true mysteries: a gift that drops into certain people from the heavens. But Hynde’s vocal expression was just as magical. She sounded like she was singing directly to you, and she had that unique slow vibrato, which could suffuse a single note with heartbreak.  

	Born in 1951 and raised in Akron, Ohio, she grew up in what’s described in the film as a “cookie-cutter postwar family.” She loved her parents but experienced their ’50s squareness as if they were aliens. At Kent State University, she was close to one of the four students killed there by the National Guard on May 4, 1970, and by the time she moved to London in the early ’70s, she was ready for anything. Which is what she got.

	She was majorly into drugs. She became a pop-music critic for New Musical Express, mostly writing scathing put-downs. But she couldn’t find a band that would have her! She met Mick Jones and attempted to work with him, but he went off and formed the Clash. She tried to join the Damned, but they weren’t biting. (She finally joined a band called the Moors Murders, who were so disreputable that they all performed in masks.) Yet she was writing songs, and her gift was pure; we hear her singing a demo of “Precious” from 1976, and the Hynde mystique is there, fully loaded.

	The only solution was to form her own band, which she did, joining forces with a bass player, Pete Farndon (they were in a relationship together), then inviting in James Honeyman-Scott, who turned out to be a karmic addition. Hynde just thought she needed a guitarist, but Honeyman-Scott, who was only 22, was as visionary a guitar player as The Edge. The ferocious drummer Martin Chambers, with his knifey sideburns, completed the quartet.

	So here was Hynde, an American girl with a smoldering stare, and her three British male back-up musicians. That sounds like a novelty, but Hynde ruled the stage with such verve, and such effortless punk-ruffian moves, that when you looked at her, you didn’t think that this was pretty much the first time in history that a woman with a guitar slung around her neck had led a rock ‘n’ roll band. She made it look like something that had always been.    
	

	The first song their producer, Nick Lowe, wanted to put out as a single was “Stop Your Sobbing,” Hynde’s cover of a 1964 track by the Kinks. If you listen to the original, it’s got a C&W-meets-British-Invasion stodginess that makes it sound like one of those slightly boring covers that filled out the Beatles’ first few albums. But Hynde makes the song as accusatory, and grandly symphonic, as a great Phil Spector track. In her hands, it’s a brand new song, one that squares with the vantage that would define the Pretenders — a grounded yearning for love, in its very imperfection, to become a higher love. As the single was getting ready to be pressed, the band still didn’t have a name, so Hynde, inspired by the Platters song “The Great Pretender,” came up with it at the last moment.

	Here’s another side of the Chrissie Hynde paradox. At 17, she became a vegetarian, and still is, mostly driven by the animal-rights aspect of it all. But as she discusses in the documentary, she also had a thing for bikers — and I don’t just mean that she liked the sexiness of riding on the back of a chopper (though she did). She was hanging out with biker-gang members who were, by her own description, homicidal, and that was part of the excitement. So when it came to her belief in punk danger, this animal-rights vegetarian wasn’t playing.  

	That spirit was the yin to her melodic yang. She wrote “Brass in Pocket,” a masterpiece of jangle, and didn’t even want to put it out as a single, though it went to number one and became defining. What lyrics! The song is so resonant that it’s like a movie, and it’s also one of the most romantic songs I’ve ever heard. It could be the anthem of a teenage girl (“‘Cause I’m…gonna make you see,/There’s nobody else here, no one like me”). It could be the anthem of anyone who’s looking for someone to fall for them.

	The Pretenders, for a while, had a satisfying life on the road. Hynde was a disciplined performer, and the guys enjoyed the perks of rock celebrity. But they indulged too much. Watching “Pretenders,” we wait for the dark side, and when it arrives it’s simple and devastating. Pete Farndon became a heroin addict, and spiraled down to the point that they had to kick him out of the band. Okay, that happened; it’s part of the rock ‘n’ roll story. He was fired from the Pretenders on June 14, 1982. Exactly two days later, James Honeyman-Scott, who was not a junkie (he was just a rock star who liked to party too much), died in his sleep of a heart attack. He was 25 years old and had been up for four nights straight, doing cocaine. This was a genuinely shocking rock death. Just like that, the band…was no longer a band.
	

	As “Pretenders” captures vividly in the conversation it features with Chrissie Hynde, she’s a straight-shooter who can be extremely prickly and defensive. She was, and still is (at 75, looking great in a black-leather jacket), a strutting rock star who hates to see herself on camera. She smashed through the rock ‘n’ roll glass ceiling before it was even named, yet she doesn’t like the label of feminist or groundbreaker or anything else of that ilk, because she doesn’t want to be stuck in the role-model box. She had a fierce bravado on stage, yet claims that she took no pride in her performances; she just thought she was getting away with something. Maybe that’s why she called herself a Pretender? In “Pretenders,” she’s as real as it gets.

schema.headline: ‘Pretenders’ Review: A Superb Portrait of Chrissie Hynde and Her Legendary Band Captures Their Incandescence…and Tragedy

title: ’60 Minutes’ Kicks Off Much-Scrutinized 59th Season With Old Ticks, Tricks
description: CBS News says it needs to push “60 Minutes” into the future if the show is to survive, but the first telecast of the 59th season following a shockin
body:
CBS News says it needs to push “60 Minutes” into the future if the show is to survive, but the first telecast of the 59th season following a shocking overhaul of its on-air and behind-the-camera staff in May and June relied on many elements from the program’s past.

	The new season of “60 Minutes” burnished stalwarts, and none of the new faces who have recently come aboard. Viewers on Sunday night got only a brief glimpse of Ross Douthat, and none of Sebastian Junger, Gianna Toboni, Trevor Phillips or Ariel Levy, but were rather greeted by three correspondents who already have an association with the program. Lesley Stahl has been with the newsmagazine since 1991, while Jon Wertheim joined the program in 2017. Norah O’Donnell was recently named a full-time correspondent on the show, but has contributed stories multiple times in the past.
	

	One of the stories even featured the old-time TV-news “hidden camera,” which many people thought went out of style after ABC News got sued in 1999 — and lost — for sending reporters to take footage at Food Lion supermarkets after lying on resumes and gaining access to tape unsanitary food practices. ABC News got tripped up on charges of trespassing and fraud, and hidden-camera reporting in the modern day is typically used mostly in public spaces or overseas, where U.S. laws don’t apply.

	Will viewers miss Cecilia Vega, Sharyn Alfonsi, or Scott Pelley? The last of that trio, all pushed out of the show following the decision to oust top producers, was on nearly every week, often crashing a story tied to events that had taken place in the days leading up to broadcast.
	

	Bari Weiss, the editor in chief of CBS News whose work at transforming the unit for modern audiences has stirred up a lot of controversy, wants “60 Minutes” to show up in more media venues and kick up livelier discussions. Other members of CBS News have felt this way as well, wondering if the program has gotten too soft or overly reliant on stories tied to the release of new books.

	There were no on-screen QR codes on Sunday’s telecast, or on-air prompts for viewers to join Stahl, Wertheim or O’Donnell for an interactive chat at CBSNews.com at some later day or time. There were no nods to listening to the stories via podcast. On Sunday morning, however, executive producer Nick Bilton sent out a note via email telling CBS News followers he would be publishing a newsletter every Monday that offered a behind-the-scenes look at the show. 

	Some of the window dressing has indeed changed. The opening logo is rendered more in black and white and has less red. The opening montage, which once looked as if spread out across the cover of a magazine, now looks as it takes place on a mobile tablet. One piece of the show did not change, at least in the first season broadcast. “The Last Minute,” a brief segment at program’s end that offers a few words about the program or its stories and was originally put into place by former executive producer Bill Owens., remains — perhaps because it has a regular sponsor.

	The stories that were presented were segments that any longtime viewer might expect. O’Donnell nabbed an interview with one of the rescued Air Force officers whose fighter jet was shot down over Iran 34 days into the war (the segment was riveting due to its access to top military personnel, as well as the pilot, but did not offer any voice or analysis outside of the armed forces). Lesley Stahl probed the world of the so-called “pardon economy,” in which attorneys and lobbyists vow to win a presidential absolution for a convicted criminal — but don’t always deliver after they get cash (a nod should be given to The Washington Sun, the news outlet previously known as NOTUS, which interviewed one of the subjects of Stahl’s story several weeks ago). And Wertheim interviewed top personnel from the Los Angeles Rams. The show routinely tries to provide a mix of stories, one based on current events or an investigation, one focused on something overseas and one feature lighter in tone.
	

	 Bilton, who seized the reins of the show as executive producer earlier this year, may not want to shake things up overmuch in a season debut. Executives at CBS News, and parent Paramount Skydance, know only too well that “60 Minutes” generated $67 million in advertising in 2025, and saw its overall audience in the 2025-2026 season rise by 9%. Those figures will be critical for CBS News to maintain, especially as audiences continue to erode for “CBS Mornings” and remain below desired levels at “CBS Evening News.”

	There are some differences, however, that the usual audience probably could not discern. Stahl’s investigation into pardons was a joint collaboration with “60 Minutes” and the CBS News investigative team, something producers at the program would likely have turned down in seasons past. Sachar Bar-On, a veteran “60 Minutes” producer, supervised the segment along with Michael Kaplan, a CBS News investigative producer and reporter. A person familiar with the show says “60 Minutes” will be “integrating more” with CBS News and its investigative unit, a move that provides more opportunity for CBS News rank-and-file doing this sort of work but also raises the specter of cost-cutting at a program with economics that already seem to work.

	On Sunday night, “60 Minutes” put its most obvious foot forward: correspondents the audience recognizes, and a story mix that doesn’t deviate wildly from the norm.

	Keep an eye on subsequent weeks of the program.  Weiss’ overhaul of the show interrupted a critical off-season period when correspondents typically try to file and finish a segment for the fall. Bilton and crew will enjoy a cushion thanks to having the new NFL season as a lead-in every Sunday for the next several weeks. Still, they won’t have the luxury of stories that may have been in the works for weeks, which may shortchange the amount of attention they can devote to segments from new on-air personnel who are still learning the ropes.

title: International Oscar Submissions: Nepal, Singapore, Israel, Romania, South Korea, Chile and More Join the List
description:
Sep 14, 2026 2:20am PT	
	

	
	International Oscar Submissions: Nepal, Singapore, Israel, Romania, South Korea, Chile and More Join the List
body:
Sep 14, 2026 2:20am PT	
	

	
	International Oscar Submissions: Nepal, Singapore, Israel, Romania, South Korea, Chile and More Join the List
	



			
			
	
						

									©Netflix/Courtesy Everett Collection
	
					


								
		
				

	The campaigns for the Oscar for international feature film are gaining momentum, with final submissions due by Oct. 1. The Oscars shortlists will be revealed on Dec. 15, with 15 international films selected to be voted on by Academy members in all branches who commit to watch all 15 films. Oscar nominations will be revealed on Jan. 21.

	This year’s entries include titles like Romania’s “Fjord,” which won the Palme d’Or at Cannes; Chile’s “The Meltdown,” which screened in Un Certain Regard; and Germany’s “Everytime,” which won Cannes’ Un Certain Regard prize. 

	France has not yet submitted a film, but faces several disparate choices. 

	Meanwhile, a new Academy rule allows any film that wins the top prize at one of the six biggest festivals — Cannes, Berlin, Venice, Sundance, Busan and Toronto — to be entered in the international feature race even without a national committee’s backing. 


			
			
	Filipiñana (Philippines)
			
										
					Image Credit: Kino Lorber				
					
				

	Rafael Manuel’s “Filipiñana” has been chosen as the official entry from the Philippines in the international feature category at the 99th Academy Awards. The film is written and directed by Manuel and is distributed by Kino Lorber.

	The film is set against a backdrop of oppressive heat and drought. The narrative follows Isabel, a 17-year-old from the provinces of the Philippines, who gets a job at a prestigious golf resort.The cast includes Jorrybell Agoto, Carmen Castellanos, Teroy Guzman, Carlitos Siguion-Reyna, Isabel Sicat and Nour Houshmand.

	Executive produced by Chinese auteur Jia Zhangke, “Filipiñana” bowed in the World Cinema Dramatic Competition at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival, where it took home the World Cinema Dramatic Special Jury Award for Creative Vision. The film went on to make its European premiere in the Perspectives section of the Berlin Film Festival.

	The film’s festival run has continued to build momentum since. It played the San Francisco International Film Festival, picking up the New Directors Award, and the Independent Film Festival of Boston, where it won the Grand Jury Prize for Best Narrative Feature. “Filipiñana” also collected the Luna de València for Best Feature Film at the Cinema Jove International Film Festival.

		
			
			
	Elephants in the Fog (Nepal)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of UTN, Les Valseurs, DGS				
					
				

	Nepal’s International Feature Film Selection Committee has chosen Abinash Bikram Shah’s “Elephants in the Fog” as the country’s entry for the 99th Academy Awards.

	The film marks Shah’s feature directorial debut and follows a Kinnar community in a Nepalese village fighting to protect itself. It premiered in the Un Certain Regard section of the Cannes Film Festival in May, where it won the section’s Jury Prize, and also picked up nominations for the Caméra d’Or and the Queer Palm. The cast is led by Pushpa Thing Lama, Deepika Yadav, Jasmine Bishwokarma, Aliz Ghimire and Dura Sanjay Kumar Gupta.

	The Oscars selection comes as “Elephants in the Fog” continues to expand its footprint in international markets. Sales company Best Friend Forever has closed deals in several territories, including MetFilm Distribution in the U.K., Filmin in Spain, Vedette in Benelux, Trigon in Switzerland, Lev Cinema in Israel, Jayantii in Australia, EFAR Films in India, PT Falcon in Indonesia and the Film Development Council of the Philippines, alongside an inflight deal with Silk Route. Those additions build on earlier deals covering France, Germany and Austria, Brazil and Nepal itself. The film is produced by Underground Talkies Nepal, Les Valseurs and Die Gesellschaft DGS.

		
			
			
	We Are All Strangers (Singapore)
			
										
					Image Credit: Giraffe Pictures				
					
				

	“We Are All Strangers,” written and directed by Anthony Chen, has been selected as Singapore‘s entry in the international feature category at the 99th Academy Awards.

	Set in contemporary Singapore, the film centers on family relationships and unexpected life changes. It stars Chen’s frequent collaborators Yeo Yann Yann and Koh Jia Ler, with Andi Lim and Regene Lim rounding out the cast. Earlier this year, it became the first Singaporean film selected for the main competition at the Berlin Film Festival.

	“We Are All Strangers” completes Chen’s Growing Up trilogy, which began with “Ilo Ilo” in 2013 and continued with “Wet Season” in 2019. The two earlier films have collectively won more than 50 international accolades, including five Golden Horse Awards, along with “Ilo Ilo‘s” Caméra d’Or win at Cannes. Both films previously served as Singapore’s Oscars entries, at the 86th and 93rd Academy Awards respectively.

		
			
			
	Tell Me Everything (Israel)
			
										
					Image Credit: Ziv Berkovich				
					
				

	Moshe Rosenthal’s “Tell Me Everything” has been voted Best Picture at Israel’s Ophir Awards, automatically making it the country’s submission for best international feature film category at the 99th Academy Awards.

	“Tell Me Everything,” set in the 1980s against the rising HIV epidemic, premiered at Sundance in the world cinema dramatic competition. It is Moshe Rosenthal’s sophomore feature. “Karaoke,” his directorial feature debut, premiered at the 2022 Tribeca Film Festival.

	“Tell Me Everything” follows Boaz (played by Yair Mazor), a 12-year-old who discovers a devastating secret about his father. Catching up with Boaz as an adult (played by “The Vanishing Soldier’s” Ido Tako), the film delves into their father-son relationship as they attempt to heal wounds and repair bonds. Assi Cohen (“Yossi & Jagger”) stars as Boaz’s father.

		
			
			
	Fjord (Romania)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Tudor Panduru				
					
				

	“Fjord,” written and directed by Cristian Mungiu, is Romania’s submission for the 2027 Oscars in the best international feature film category, having been unanimously chosen by the country’s selection committee.

	The film premiered in the official competition at the Cannes Film Festival, where it won the Palme d’Or for best film, the FIPRESCI Prize, the Ecumenical Jury Prize, the Prix de la Citoyenneté and the François Chalais Prize.

	Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve star in the lead roles, with cinematography by Tudor Vladimir Panduru, editing by Mircea Olteanu, and production design by Simona Pădurețu.

		
			
			
	Aontas (Ireland)
			
										
					Image Credit: Púca Pictures				
					
				

	“Aontas,” the Irish-language heist thriller from director Damian McCann, has been chosen as Ireland’s entry for the best international feature film category at the 2027 Academy Awards.

	The film was selected by the Irish Film & TV Academy (IFTA) and a committee including “Evil Dead Rise” director Lee Cronin, “Derry Girls” creator Lisa McGee, BAFTA-nominated director Brian Kirk (“Game of Thrones), BAFTA nominated director Kathryn Ferguson (“Nothing Compares”), Emmy-winning actress and filmmaker Aisha Tyler (“Friends”), actress Fionnuala Flaherty (“Kneecap”) and IFTA chief executive Áine Moriarty.

	Told in reverse chronology, “Aontas” follows three unlikely thieves, led by a woman on the verge of a breakdown, who rob a rural Irish bank. Opening in the tragic aftermath of the heist-gone-wrong. What starts as a poorly executed robbery becomes a portrait of a wilful woman trapped in her own past. It stars Carrie Crowley (“The Quiet Girl “), Bríd Brennan, Eva-Jane Gaffney, Seán T. Ó Meallaigh, Marcus Lamb and Art Parkinson.

		
			
			
	The Meltdown (Chile)
			
										
					Image Credit: 'The Meltdown'  Courtesy of Mubi				
					
				

	Chile’s Film Academy has selected “The Meltdown” (“El deshielo”) by Manuela Martelli, her post-Pinochet mystery drama set in an Andes ski resort, to represent the country in the Best International Feature category at the 2027 Academy Awards. Martelli’s follow-up to her acclaimed drama “Chile, 1976” had its world premiere at Cannes’ prominent strand Un Certain Regard this year.

	“The Meltdown” stars Maya O’Rourke – in her film debut – who plays a nine-year-old at her family’s ski resort who witnesses unsettling events that will test her loyalties. Other cast members are Paulina Urrutia, Mauricio Pešutić, Paula Zúñiga, Marcela Salinas and Lautaro Cantillana.

		
			
			
	All of a Sudden (Japan)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Neon, Cannes Film Festival				
					
				

	Hamaguchi Ryusuke‘s “All of a Sudden” has been selected as Japan’s entry in the international feature category at the 99th Academy Awards, the Motion Picture Producers Association of Japan (Eiren) has revealed.

	The selection marks the second time a Hamaguchi film has represented Japan in the category, five years after “Drive My Car” won the international feature Oscar and picked up nominations for best picture, director and adapted screenplay at the 94th Academy Awards.

	“All of a Sudden” is a France-Japan co-production made with backing from Germany and Belgium, shot largely in Paris. The film draws on “When Life Suddenly Takes a Turn: Twenty Letters Between a Philosopher With Terminal Cancer and a Medical Anthropologist,” a book of correspondence by Miyano Makiko and Isono Maho. It follows Marie-Lou Fontaine (Virginie Efira), who runs a nursing home outside Paris and pushes to adopt a more dignity-focused model of elderly care, and Morisaki Mari (Okamoto Tao), a Japanese theater director undergoing cancer treatment. Nagatsuka Kyōzō and Kurosaki Kōdai round out the cast.

		
			
			
	Everytime (Germany)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of The Barricades				
					
				

	Sandra Wollner’s “Everytime” has been selected as Germany’s entry for the Academy Award for best international feature film.

	The film’s synopsis reads as follows: The last photograph Jessie took shows the sun over Berlin. It hangs there as if nothing had happened. But Ella has lost her daughter. What remains is Jessie’s younger sister and a complicated relationship with the boy everyone blames. The unlikely trio ends up on a family holiday that never really existed. Under the shimmering sun of Tenerife, memory and the present become inseparably intertwined. The ghosts are everywhere.

	“Everytime” celebrated its world premiere at the 79th Cannes Film Festival in May. Wollner’s third feature film, for which she also wrote the screenplay, was selected for the Un Certain Regard sidebar where it won the Prix Un Certain Regard, the section’s top award. Cannes was followed by invitations to the Sydney Film Festival and the Karlovy Vary Film Festival, among others. At the Sarajevo Film Festival, “Everytime” was awarded the Heart of Sarajevo Grand Prize. Its North American premiere will follow in September at the Toronto Film Festival. Other festival appearances include the New York Film Festival.

		
			
			
	Becoming Human (Cambodia)
			
										
					Image Credit: Anti-Archive				
					
				

	The Cambodia Oscar Selection Committee (COSC) has selected “Becoming Human,” directed by Polen Ly, as the country’s official submission for the international feature film category at the 99th Academy Awards.

	The film follows Thida, the spirit guardian of an aging cinema slated for demolition, as she weighs the choice of rebirth against her existence as a ghost. Her bond with Hai, a living man she meets along the way, pushes her to confront both her spiritual fate and a country in the midst of sweeping social change.

	“Becoming Human” is Ly’s debut feature. He previously made the short film “Further and Further Away” in 2022 and the documentary “Until the Orchid Blooms,” which premiered at IDFA in 2024 and won the grand prize at the Taiwan International Documentary Festival in 2026. The cast is led by 15-year-old newcomer and dance student Savorn Serak alongside Piseth Chhun, who won the Venice Horizons award for best actor in 2021 for his role in Kavich Neang’s “White Building.”

		
			
			
	Possible Love (South Korea)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Netflix, Venice Film Festival				
					
				

	The Korean Film Council (KOFIC) has selected “Possible Love,” directed by Lee Chang-dong, as South Korea‘s official entry for the international feature film category at the 2027 Academy Awards.

	“Possible Love” marks Lee’s first feature in eight years, following “Burning,” “Poetry” and “Secret Sunshine.” The film centers on two married couples whose lives intersect after a funeral: Mi-ok and her laid-off husband Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu), who live quietly with their young son Cheol, and Ye-ji, a filmmaker making a documentary about workers who lost their jobs, and her husband Sang-woo (Zo In-sung). When Mi-ok agrees to be filmed by Ye-ji, the two women grow close, while Mi-ok finds herself unsettled by an attraction to Sang-woo. As the two couples’ worlds overlap, cracks begin to surface in both marriages.

	In its evaluation, the committee cited the film’s polished craftsmanship and the clarity of its directorial vision, pointing to the tone and mise-en-scène that sustain a sense of pressure throughout the story. The drama was described as prompting reflection on gentle forms of violence, incomplete freedom and the nature of true happiness, alongside a labor movement sequence that the committee said captured layered social undercurrents.

		
			
			
	Like a Limbless Tree (Turkey)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Tekhne Film				
					
				

	“Like a Limbless Tree,” an intimate social drama directed by Tunç Davut, has been selected as Turkey‘s entry for the Academy Award for best international feature film.

	Davut, whose previous works include the 2015 drama “Entanglement and TV series “Serçe” and “Kinali Kuzular,” delves into the fragility of human existence against a backdrop of the theme of immigration in “Like a Limbless Tree.” The film is produced by Istanbul-based Tekhne Film and stars Ali Ipin, Fayyaz Duman and Selen Kurtaran.

	Davut’s drama – which won an award at the Bosphorus Film Festival and was selected for the Antalya Golden Orange Film Festival and the Ankara Film Festival – is about a retired engineer named Refik whose life changes forever after being diagnosed with a terminal disease just as his Syrian caregiver disappears while attempting to flee to Europe, leaving him in charge of her two children.

		
			
			
	How to Divorce During the War (Lithuania)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of New Europe Film Sales				
					
				

	Andrius Blaževičius’ “How to Divorce During the War” has been selected as Lithuania’s entry for the Academy Award for best international feature film.

	Blaževičius’ third feature won the directing award in the World Cinema Dramatic Competition at the Sundance Film Festival. The film was picked up for theatrical distribution in North America by Zeitgeist Films, in association with Kino Lorber, and will be released on Aug. 21.

	Set in Vilnius in 2022, it’s a story of a high-flying executive Marija, who chooses the worst possible moment for an honest conversation with her husband Vytas about divorcing – just one day before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine goes into full scale. Now the couple must navigate the process of separation as it collides with a refugee and mid-life crisis.

		
			
			
	First Light (Australia)
			
										
					Image Credit: International Film Festival Rotterdam				
					
				

	“First Light,” the feature directorial debut of Filipino-Australian filmmaker James J. Robinson, has been selected as Australia’s entry in the international feature film category at the 99th Academy Awards, marking the first Filipino-Australian co-production and the first Tagalog-language film the country has ever submitted for Oscar consideration. 

	The film follows Sister Yolanda (Ruby Ruiz), a nun and nurse leading a peaceful, disciplined existence until a young construction worker’s suspicious death draws her into uncovering corruption reaching both the community’s wealthy elite and the church she has devoted her life to.

	The film premiered at the 2025 Melbourne International Film Festival, where Robinson took home the best Australian director award. It later screened in the main competition lineup at Marrakech and went on to play the New Zealand International Film Festival, the International Film Festival Rotterdam and the Glasgow Film Festival.

		
	
	


	
		More from Variety

title: Lindsay Clancy's Ex Patrick Clancy Seen With New Wife in Hamptons After Mistrial
description:
Patrick Clancy
                          Hamptons Coffee Run With New Wife After Mistrial
body:
Patrick Clancy
                          Hamptons Coffee Run With New Wife After Mistrial
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 13, 2026
                            5:00 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Patrick Clancy and his new wife are continuing to move forward after the mistrial in Lindsay Clancy's murder case ... stepping out for a low-key Hamptons coffee run.
      
    
            TMZ obtained a photo of Patrick and Rachel Danis inside the Milk Pail on Saturday, where the two appeared to be grabbing drinks and browsing the shop.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Patrick kept it casual in a pink polo and shorts, while Rachel stood nearby a few feet behind him.
      

            The sighting comes just over a week after a judge declared a mistrial in Lindsay's case after jurors said they were hopelessly deadlocked.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported, Patrick later said through his attorney there would "never be closure" after losing his three children ... adding it's something he'll never recover from.
      
    
            Rachel was spotted solo in Manhattan earlier this week -- her first public sighting since the mistrial -- but this appears to be the first time we've seen Patrick and his new wife out together since the case ended in a hung jury.
